details.name: Distributed Systems

families.title: Concurrency and Mutual Exclusion
families.question: Concurrency allows multiple activities to overlap. Mutual exclusion makes a critical section accessible to at most one participant at a time, avoiding unsafe interleavings.

families.title: Distributed Algorithms
families.question: A distributed algorithm reaches a global outcome using only local state and communication. In an answer, state exactly what is guaranteed—such as election of one leader—not merely that nodes “agree.”

families.title: Distributed Foundations
families.question: A distributed system coordinates independent computers through a network to provide a service. Good answers connect its benefits to its new problems: no shared clock, partial failure and network delay.

families.title: GPU and Parallel Programming
families.question: GPU programming uses many lightweight workers to perform similar operations on different data. The key question is whether iterations are independent enough to run concurrently and whether memory transfer overwhelms the gain.

families.title: HPC, Storage and Large Data
families.question: High-performance computing (HPC) combines resources to solve large computations quickly. Large-data systems must also store, move and recover data efficiently; compute speed alone cannot fix an I/O bottleneck.

families.title: Message Passing
families.question: Message passing lets separate processes exchange requests, replies or events. The core task is to describe delivery, ordering and duplicate handling rather than assuming a call behaves like a local function call.

families.title: Replication and Consistency
families.question: Replication maintains copies of data or service state. It can improve read capacity and availability, but updates must be propagated and readers need a stated consistency guarantee.

families.title: Transactions and Fault Tolerance
families.question: A transaction groups operations into a meaningful unit. Fault tolerance preserves an agreed service property despite specified faults; it does not mean that every request succeeds during every outage.

sheets.title: Concurrency and Mutual Exclusion
sheets.purpose: Concurrency allows multiple activities to overlap. Mutual exclusion makes a critical section accessible to at most one participant at a time, avoiding unsafe interleavings.
refresher: Critical section needs mutual exclusion/progress/bounded waiting.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: Balance=10. Two withdrawals each read 10 and write 7; the final balance is 7 though £6 was withdrawn. A mutex makes one withdrawal complete before the other reads. In a distributed service, the lock manager must not grant two leases and needs expiry/recovery rules.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Two threads execute x=x+1 when x=7. Show a losing interleaving and repair it while stating the required critical-section properties. [8 marks]
practice.route: Each increment reads, computes and writes. T1 reads 7; T2 reads 7; both compute 8; T1 writes 8; T2 writes 8: one increment is lost. Put the read-modify-write inside one mutex (or use an atomic fetch-add), so mutual exclusion holds. The mechanism must also allow progress when no thread is inside and bounded waiting so one contender is not postponed indefinitely.
practice.answer: Each increment reads, computes and writes. T1 reads 7; T2 reads 7; both compute 8; T1 writes 8; T2 writes 8: one increment is lost. Put the read-modify-write inside one mutex (or use an atomic fetch-add), so mutual exclusion holds. The mechanism must also allow progress when no thread is inside and bounded waiting so one contender is not postponed indefinitely.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: T1 locks A then waits for B; T2 locks B then waits for A. Diagnose the deadlock and give a design-level cure. [8 marks]
practice.route: All four Coffman conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption and circular wait. Establish one global order, e.g. always acquire A before B; then T2 cannot take B first, breaking circular wait. Release in reverse order and keep critical sections small. A timeout may recover operationally but is not proof that the design has eliminated deadlock.

A timeout may recover operationally but is not proof that the design has eliminated deadlock.

sheets.title: Distributed Algorithms
sheets.purpose: A distributed algorithm reaches a global outcome using only local state and communication. In an answer, state exactly what is guaranteed—such as election of one leader—not merely that nodes “agree.”
refresher: Consensus needs agreement/validity/termination under named failures.
Lamport one-way causality, vectors reveal concurrency.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: Three ring nodes have IDs 4, 9 and 6. Each sends its ID around the ring and forwards only the largest ID seen. ID 9 returns to node 9, so it declares itself leader and announces this. Safety depends on IDs being unique; progress depends on the ring forwarding messages.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Processes A and B send to C; A’s event a happens-before its send, and C receives A’s message before sending to B. Compare Lamport and vector clocks for deciding whether a concurrent B event caused C’s send. [9 marks]
practice.route: Lamport clocks increment locally and set receive time above the carried value, so L(a)<L(C-send) establishes an order but the converse does not establish causality: ordered scalar values can be concurrent. A vector clock increments its own component and merges component-wise on receive. If V(B-event) and V(C-send) are incomparable (each has a greater component), they are concurrent; if every component of B is ≤ C and one is strict, B happened-before C.
practice.answer: Lamport clocks increment locally and set receive time above the carried value, so L(a)<L(C-send) establishes an order but the converse does not establish causality: ordered scalar values can be concurrent. A vector clock increments its own component and merges component-wise on receive. If V(B-event) and V(C-send) are incomparable (each has a greater component), they are concurrent; if every component of B is ≤ C and one is strict, B happened-before C.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A leader crashes after proposing a commit to replicas. State the consensus properties and a safe response under partial failure. [8 marks]
practice.route: Agreement means no two correct replicas decide differently; validity constrains decisions to proposed values; termination is conditional on the failure/timing model. A timeout gives suspicion, not proof of crash, so surviving replicas use a quorum/election protocol and durable log to select a leader that preserves the highest safe proposal before deciding. Never let two isolated groups each commit a different value.

Never let two isolated groups each commit a different value.

sheets.title: Distributed Foundations
sheets.purpose: A distributed system coordinates independent computers through a network to provide a service. Good answers connect its benefits to its new problems: no shared clock, partial failure and network delay.
refresher: No global clock and partial failures.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: A photo service stores files on two servers. A client uploads to server A; A copies to B. This can improve availability if A later crashes, but copying needs network messages and the two copies may briefly differ. The design must decide whether the client waits for both copies or accepts a later update.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A client times out after sending payment ID P17. The server may have charged the card, but the reply was lost. Design the retry protocol. [9 marks]
practice.route: The network can delay, duplicate or lose messages; silence is not proof of crash. Put P17 in a durable idempotency record before/with the side effect. On a retry, the server returns the recorded completed/pending result rather than charging again; the client may poll status using P17. This preserves safety (at most one charge) while availability depends on recovery/replication.
practice.answer: The network can delay, duplicate or lose messages; silence is not proof of crash. Put P17 in a durable idempotency record before/with the side effect. On a retry, the server returns the recorded completed/pending result rather than charging again; the client may poll status using P17. This preserves safety (at most one charge) while availability depends on recovery/replication.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A replica returns an old profile immediately after a network partition. Explain safety versus liveness and choose a policy for a bank balance. [8 marks]
practice.route: Safety means nothing bad happens, e.g. conflicting balance updates are not both accepted; liveness means a request eventually completes. During a partition, serving every write at every side improves availability but can lose a single-current-balance guarantee. For a bank balance choose a quorum/leader policy that rejects or delays unsafe writes, then use versioning/log recovery after the partition.

For a bank balance choose a quorum/leader policy that rejects or delays unsafe writes, then use versioning/log recovery after the partition.

sheets.title: GPU and Parallel Programming
sheets.purpose: GPU programming uses many lightweight workers to perform similar operations on different data. The key question is whether iterations are independent enough to run concurrently and whether memory transfer overwhelms the gain.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: To add arrays A and B of length n, worker i computes C[i]=A[i]+B[i] when i<n. Each worker writes a distinct C[i], so no lock is needed. The design is less effective if n is tiny or host-to-device copying dominates the arithmetic.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: For vector addition of n=1000 with blockDim.x=256 , give the grid size, last valid index and a CUDA-style kernel guard. [8 marks]
practice.route: Grid size is ceil(1000/256)=4 blocks, launching 1024 threads. i=blockIdx.x*blockDim.x+threadIdx.x; if(i<1000) c[i]=a[i]+b[i]; . The last valid element index is 999; threads 1000–1023 must not access memory. Consecutive threads should read consecutive array elements for coalescing.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Sum 1024 floats with blocks of 256. Describe a two-stage reduction and its synchronisation. [9 marks]
practice.route: Each of four blocks loads one element per thread (or a grid-stride subset) into shared memory; after each stride-halving addition, use a block barrier before a value is read in the next stride. Thread 0 writes one partial sum per block, so stage one produces four partials; a second kernel/block reduces those to one sum. Do not use a block barrier to coordinate blocks: it has block scope.

sheets.title: HPC, Storage and Large Data
sheets.purpose: High-performance computing (HPC) combines resources to solve large computations quickly. Large-data systems must also store, move and recover data efficiently; compute speed alone cannot fix an I/O bottleneck.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: To count events in a 1 TB log, split files across workers. Each worker counts locally; a final stage adds the counts. If all records for one customer key go to one worker, that worker delays completion: use a better partition key or split that hot key before aggregation.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A job is 10% serial and 90% perfectly parallel. Compute Amdahl’s ideal speedup at 16 processors and explain why 16× is impossible. [8 marks]
practice.route: S(16)=1/(0.10+0.90/16)=1/0.15625=6.4. The serial fraction caps asymptotic speedup at 10, even before communication, synchronisation and I/O. Profile first: reducing the serial coordinator or overlapping I/O can improve the bound; adding processors to a fixed serial phase cannot.
practice.answer: S(16)=1/(0.10+0.90/16)=1/0.15625=6.4. The serial fraction caps asymptotic speedup at 10, even before communication, synchronisation and I/O. Profile first: reducing the serial coordinator or overlapping I/O can improve the bound; adding processors to a fixed serial phase cannot.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Adding nodes makes a data pipeline slower. Give a measurement-led diagnosis across compute, memory, network and parallel storage. [9 marks]
practice.route: Measure CPU utilisation, memory bandwidth/cache misses, network shuffle time, metadata operations and read/write throughput per node. Small-file metadata contention or poorly striped shared output can dominate despite spare CPU. Combine large files/collective I/O, choose an appropriate stripe count, batch metadata operations and avoid all workers contending for one writer. Validate by comparing phase timings before/after, not node count alone.

Small-file metadata contention or poorly striped shared output can dominate despite spare CPU. Combine large files/collective I/O, choose an appropriate stripe count, batch metadata operations and avoid all workers contending for one writer. Validate by comparing phase timings before/after, not node count alone.

sheets.title: Message Passing
sheets.purpose: Message passing lets separate processes exchange requests, replies or events. The core task is to describe delivery, ordering and duplicate handling rather than assuming a call behaves like a local function call.
refresher: Format, correlation ID, order, ACK and retry define protocol.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: A client sends “reserve seat 17” with ID R9. The server reserves the seat but its reply is lost. The client retries R9. The server records R9 and replies “already reserved for this request,” rather than reserving a second seat. This gives a practical exactly-once effect at the application level.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A payment command reaches the bank, which performs the debit, then crashes before ACK; the client retries after an ACK loss. Define the message protocol so the debit happens once. [9 marks]
practice.route: Include command ID, sender, amount and correlation ID. The bank durably records the ID and outcome atomically with the debit; duplicates return the stored result. ACKs may be retried and messages reordered, so the client correlates replies by ID and uses a status query after timeout. A queue decouples sender/receiver but does not create exactly-once processing by itself.
practice.answer: Include command ID, sender, amount and correlation ID. The bank durably records the ID and outcome atomically with the debit; duplicates return the stored result. ACKs may be retried and messages reordered, so the client correlates replies by ID and uses a status query after timeout. A queue decouples sender/receiver but does not create exactly-once processing by itself.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: Compare a synchronous RPC with an asynchronous queue for a slow image-processing service. [8 marks]
practice.route: RPC blocks the caller awaiting a reply and is simple for immediate validation, but couples availability and can exhaust callers during slowdown. A queue accepts a durable command, lets workers scale/retry and returns a job ID; it needs correlation, idempotence, back-pressure and status handling. Choose queueing for a long task where delayed completion is acceptable.

A queue accepts a durable command, lets workers scale/retry and returns a job ID; it needs correlation, idempotence, back-pressure and status handling. Choose queueing for a long task where delayed completion is acceptable.

sheets.title: Replication and Consistency
sheets.purpose: Replication maintains copies of data or service state. It can improve read capacity and availability, but updates must be propagated and readers need a stated consistency guarantee.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: With N=3, choose W=2 and R=2. Since 2+2>3, any read quorum overlaps any completed write quorum. After a write reaches two replicas, a two-replica read sees at least one updated copy. A client reading one replica instead may still see an old value.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: For N=3 replicas, choose R and W for a strong quorum intersection and calculate the condition. Explain what it does not solve. [8 marks]
practice.route: Choose R=2,W=2: R+W=4>N, so every read quorum intersects every write quorum in at least one replica. With appropriate version/leader protocol this supports fresh reads of acknowledged writes. It does not itself resolve two writes, guarantee availability during a partition or make a stale replica up-to-date without repair.

With appropriate version/leader protocol this supports fresh reads of acknowledged writes. It does not itself resolve two writes, guarantee availability during a partition or make a stale replica up-to-date without repair.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A partition lets two clinics edit the same patient address under eventual consistency. Give a convergent conflict policy and contrast it with linearizability. [9 marks]
practice.route: Eventual consistency permits each side to accept updates and later converge. Carry versions/vector metadata and define a domain rule: for an address, retain both conflicting values and require reconciliation (or use a documented last-writer rule only if its loss is acceptable). Linearizability instead makes each operation appear at one instant and would reject/wait on one side to avoid concurrent visible writes.

Linearizability instead makes each operation appear at one instant and would reject/wait on one side to avoid concurrent visible writes.

sheets.title: Transactions and Fault Tolerance
sheets.purpose: A transaction groups operations into a meaningful unit. Fault tolerance preserves an agreed service property despite specified faults; it does not mean that every request succeeds during every outage.
refresher: 2PC durable prepare then decision but blocks.

practice.title: Worked examples and method extensions
practice.prompt: A transfer debits A by €20 and credits B by €20. The coordinator asks both databases to prepare, then records and broadcasts commit only if both can commit. If B cannot prepare, it aborts and A does not debit. If the coordinator fails after prepare, participants consult recovery/decision information rather than guessing.

practice.title: Practice question 1 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: In 2PC, all participants have durably voted YES and the coordinator crashes before sending its decision. Explain the states, recovery evidence and blocking risk. [9 marks]
practice.route: Each participant has logged PREPARED and holds locks after YES; it cannot unilaterally abort because another participant may have committed. On recovery the coordinator reads its durable log: a logged decision is retransmitted; no decision requires the protocol’s safe recovery path/coordination. This is why 2PC can block under coordinator failure despite atomicity.
practice.answer: Each participant has logged PREPARED and holds locks after YES; it cannot unilaterally abort because another participant may have committed. On recovery the coordinator reads its durable log: a logged decision is retransmitted; no decision requires the protocol’s safe recovery path/coordination. This is why 2PC can block under coordinator failure despite atomicity.

practice.title: Practice question 2 [medium/hard]
practice.prompt: A transfer debits A then the service crashes before crediting B; the client retries. Give a transactional recovery design. [8 marks]
practice.route: Use one ACID transaction where possible: log intent and both updates, commit atomically, then return a durable transaction ID. Recovery redoes committed work or undoes incomplete work from the write-ahead log; retry with the same ID returns the recorded result. In distributed settings, a saga/compensation must be explicit and idempotent.

Recovery redoes committed work or undoes incomplete work from the write-ahead log; retry with the same ID returns the recorded result. In distributed settings, a saga/compensation must be explicit and idempotent.
